hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
In a nursing home filled with people in their 90s—many too frail to walk without help or stand up from a chair on their own—researchers decided to put them on a weight-training program.
Not light calisthenics. Not gentle stretching. High-intensity progressive resistance training, three times a week, with loads that eventually reached about 80% of each person’s maximum. The results, published in JAMA in 1990 by Maria Fiatarone and colleagues, upended long-held assumptions about aging and muscle.
Ten frail, institutionalized volunteers (average age 90, some as old as 96) trained their quadriceps for just eight weeks. Their strength exploded—an average gain of 174%, with some individuals more than tripling their starting numbers. Mid-thigh muscle cross-sectional area increased by roughly 9%. More importantly, function improved: tandem gait speed rose nearly 50%. Several participants who had needed canes or arm support to rise from a chair no longer did. Attendance was extraordinarily high; these were not people who were easily motivated by abstract health advice, yet they showed up and pushed themselves.
The study demonstrated something radical for its time: the muscles of people in their tenth decade still possess remarkable plasticity. They respond to progressive overload with substantial gains in strength, size, and real-world mobility—changes that meaningfully restored independence and reduced the burden of frailty. The relative magnitude of adaptation was comparable to what much younger adults experience under similar training.
In short, the experiment proved that chronological age, even extreme age accompanied by chronic disease and institutionalization, does not erase the body’s capacity to grow stronger. Strength training could reverse a large portion of the functional decline once considered inevitable.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker dug up a 1990 study from JAMA. Researchers put frail nursing-home residents, average age 90, on proper weight training three times a week, working up to about 80% of their max.

In eight weeks their leg strength went up 174% on average. Walking speed improved by nearly half, and a few who'd needed a cane or a hand to get out of a chair didn't anymore.

If muscle still answers at 90, it'll answer at 50 or 60. It's never too late to start. Start light, build up slowly, and get your GP's tick first if you've got a heart or joint problem.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
For decades, plant-based advocates insisted saturated fat was a dietary poison that clogged arteries and shortened lives. Then one of the largest nutrition studies ever conducted arrived and refused to cooperate.
The Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study followed 135,335 adults aged 35–70 from 18 countries spanning five continents—high-, middle-, and low-income nations alike. Over a median of 7.4 years, researchers documented nearly 5,800 deaths and almost 4,800 major cardiovascular events. Diets were assessed with food-frequency questionnaires, and participants were grouped by quintiles of carbohydrate and fat intake.
The results, published in The Lancet in 2017, upended conventional wisdom. Higher total fat intake was linked to a 23% lower risk of total mortality. Saturated fat specifically showed an inverse association: those in the highest quintile had a 14% lower risk of dying from any cause compared with the lowest quintile, plus a reduced risk of stroke. Total fat and saturated fat showed no significant link to myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death. By contrast, the highest carbohydrate intakes were associated with a 28% higher risk of total mortality.
The authors noted that these findings stood in contrast to longstanding dietary guidelines that had demonized saturated fat. The sheer scale and geographic diversity of PURE made the results hard to dismiss as a niche Western phenomenon.
Plant-based advocates and low-fat proponents reacted with urgency. Critiques poured out from academic nutrition centers and plant-focused organizations, emphasizing confounding by poverty (high-carb diets in poorer regions), the limitations of observational data, and self-reported intake. Some argued the study changed nothing or was misleading. The intensity of the pushback underscored how directly PURE challenged decades of messaging that had elevated plant foods while casting animal fats as uniquely harmful.
In a field long dominated by consensus rather than consistent outcome data, PURE’s size and findings forced a reckoning: saturated fat was not the mortality risk it had been portrayed to be.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker pointed back to the PURE study: 135,000 adults in 18 countries, followed for about seven years, published in The Lancet in 2017.

Higher total fat was linked to a 23% lower risk of dying, and the people eating the most saturated fat had a 14% lower risk than those eating the least. The highest carb intakes were linked to a 28% higher risk.

It's observational, and critics point out high-carb diets are more common in poorer countries, so it's a link, not proof. But it's a fair reason not to fear eggs, meat and butter on a working plate. If you've got heart trouble, talk it through with your doctor.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church significantly shaped early American nutrition science and the professionalization of dietetics through its 19th-century health reform movement. Shortly after the church’s 1863 organization, cofounder Ellen G. White promoted temperance and a plant-centered diet of grains, fruits, nuts, and vegetables, drawing on biblical references such as Genesis 1:29. In 1866 Adventists established the Western Health Reform Institute in Battle Creek, Michigan (later the Battle Creek Sanitarium). Under the direction of John Harvey Kellogg (trained with Adventist support), the institution became a major health center emphasizing vegetarian meals, hydrotherapy, and lifestyle changes. Kellogg and colleagues developed practical foods including flaked cereals (precursors to corn flakes), peanut butter, granola, and early meat analogs, helping shift American breakfast patterns away from heavy meat and toward grain-based options. These innovations commercialized vegetarian foods on a large scale. 
Lenna Frances Cooper, chief dietitian at the Battle Creek Sanitarium and trained under Kellogg, co-founded the American Dietetic Association (now the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics) in 1917 and helped establish formal dietetics education grounded in vegetarian principles. Adventists later founded Loma Linda University, which has offered nutrition programs since the early 20th century and conducted the large Adventist Health Studies. These prospective cohort studies of tens of thousands of Adventists provided key epidemiological evidence linking vegetarian diets to lower rates of heart disease, certain cancers, diabetes, and longer lifespan. 
The church continues to favor vegetarianism as part of its broader “health message,” viewing the body as a temple and encouraging plant-based eating for physical and spiritual reasons. While not a mandatory doctrine for membership, it is strongly promoted through institutions, food companies, education, and research, contributing both historical food innovations and ongoing scientific data on plant-based diets.

In 2019, a team of rigorous methodologists—including Gordon Guyatt, the physician who coined the term “evidence-based medicine”—dropped a bombshell: the long-standing claims linking red meat to heart disease and cancer rested on extremely weak evidence.
Published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, the NutriRECS consortium’s series of systematic reviews and guidelines examined roughly 180 observational studies covering millions of people plus the limited randomized trial data available. Using the GRADE framework (which Guyatt helped develop and which is now the standard for rating evidence certainty at organizations like the WHO), the authors rated the evidence linking unprocessed red meat and processed meat to cardiovascular disease, cancer, and mortality as low to very low certainty. Absolute risk reductions from cutting back by three servings per week were tiny and often trivial. The panel therefore issued a weak recommendation that adults continue their current levels of red and processed meat consumption rather than be told to cut back for health reasons.
The authors emphasized transparency: most people value the taste and convenience of meat enough that, given the uncertain and small benefits of reduction, continuing current habits is reasonable. They deliberately excluded animal welfare and environmental concerns, focusing only on human health outcomes.
The reaction from plant-based advocacy groups was swift and aggressive. The Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine (PCRM), a prominent vegan-oriented organization, petitioned the Federal Trade Commission, arguing that the journal’s promotion of the findings was misleading advertising. Groups such as the True Health Initiative also pressed the journal to retract or withhold the papers before publication, citing alleged conflicts and methodological disagreement. Critics highlighted past industry ties of some authors and contended that GRADE was being misapplied to nutrition data. The intensity of the campaign underscored how deeply the weak-evidence conclusion challenged entrenched dietary dogma.
Guyatt and his colleagues stood by the work, arguing that honest assessment of evidence quality—rather than overconfident guidelines based on low-certainty data—better serves the public. The episode remains a stark illustration of how weak observational associations have been treated as settled science on red meat.

Higher meat intake tracks with longer lives—and the usual “plant-based is better” story collapses under population data.
Across 175 countries, total meat supply (all flesh meats and offal, grams per person per day from FAO data, 2011–2013 averages) showed a strong positive correlation with life expectancy at birth (Pearson r ≈ 0.710) and at age 5, plus a clear inverse link with under-5 child mortality (r ≈ −0.746). Carbohydrate crops (cereals, starchy roots, and sugars) showed only a weak, non-significant or negative association. Meat intake explained at least half the variance in the key scatterplots. These patterns held across developed and developing countries, most WHO regions, and both high- and low-meat groups. 
The authors directly tested the usual confounders that plant-based advocates often cite. Partial correlations kept the meat–life-expectancy relationship significant after controlling for total caloric intake, urbanization, GDP (purchasing-power parity), adult obesity prevalence, and carbohydrate-crop intake. Stepwise linear regression selected meat—not carbohydrate crops—as a significant independent predictor. Education level was also examined where data allowed. In short, the association did not disappear once wealth, energy balance, city living, obesity, or carbohydrate volume were held constant. The researchers noted that many vegetarian longevity studies suffer from non-representative samples (e.g., health-conscious Adventists) and incomplete lifestyle adjustment; their broader ecological approach was designed to reduce that bias.
This is population-level ecological evidence, not proof of individual causation, and residual factors (healthcare quality, sanitation, smoking, activity, genetics, food processing) remain possible. Still, it undercuts the narrative that simply swapping meat for grains and plants reliably extends life. High-meat traditional pastoral cultures (Mongolian nomads, certain Arctic and African herding groups) contrast with long-standing cereal-dominant agricultural societies where meat was scarcer; the global data align more with the former pattern than with modern low-meat prescriptions.

outsiders.text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. (quoting @karpathy: "Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.")

outsiders.text:
AI is automating coding. So why are software developer job postings on the rise? | Corynn Winston, CNBC

U.S. software development job postings have risen since February 2025, the launch date for Anthropic's Claude Code, even as overall job postings fell, complicating predictions that AI would rapidly erase demand for developers.

Concerns about the future of the software development career are well-founded, and intensified as companies adopted AI-powered coding tools, especially as those tools keep getting better. As far back as 2023, Microsoft's software development platform GitHub said that on projects where AI was available, it was close to writing half of all code.

Some AI experts claim AI-written code across the entire GitHub platform has now passed the halfway mark. GitHub has not confirmed that, but in October it did report that one in three "pull requests" — the process in which coders that collaborate on development propose code changes for projects — now involve an AI agent. A year ago, GitHub said that number was fewer than one in 10. "If that pace holds, within the next two years, most of the code pushed to GitHub could be written by an agent. Much of it may never be fully read by a human," it stated.

Labor market researchers say that against this backdrop, the profession is evolving rather than disappearing. Data from Indeed Hiring Lab shows that U.S. software-development job postings have risen nearly 15% since February 2025, bucking both the overall job market and the coding data.

Some economic experts are pointing to the rebound in software job postings as confirmation for a glass half-full view of AI and the job market. "It wasn't that long ago that we were reading the headline that there will be no more need for software developers," Eric Kutcher, North America chair at McKinsey, said during a recent interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." Instead, he said, as companies are producing more code than ever before, software developers who work with AI remain in high demand. "We're seeing much more growth in the places we thought we were gonna see the biggest displacement," Kutcher said.

Recent research on AI and the future of jobs from McKinsey Global Institute notes that the earlier decline in the software developer field was not solely an AI story. While in recent years AI has been automating software-development tasks, the rebound comes after a steep drop from a 2022 hiring peak, when technology companies pulled back after a pandemic-era surge in hiring.

But even after the recovery, software-development job postings remain about 27.5% below their pre-pandemic level, according to Indeed Hiring Lab data. Importantly, the increase is concentrated in senior-level roles and more experienced AI-oriented positions. Indeed Hiring Lab found that senior roles accounted for 71% of the increase in software-development postings between May 2025 and May 2026. Job titles that mention AI accounted for 37% of the increase.

AI tools may be allowing companies to produce code more quickly than developers could on their own. GitHub leaders have said in the past that as much if not more than 80% of code could eventually be written by AI, especially as developers become more comfortable working with AI tools. But that also could mean the demand for workers is concentrated on those who can evaluate AI-generated code or problems and connect new tools to an organization's broader technology systems.

Sneha Puri, an economist at Indeed Hiring Lab, said companies are realizing that even if AI can handle some technical coding tasks, they still need developers to oversee that work, refine products and help clients integrate the technology into their day to day operations. One example, she said, is the growing need for workers who can help businesses apply AI tools beyond simply building them.

Early gains in AI era may not last, young workers remain at risk

Right now, factors like the ones cited by Puri are helping software developers to be among winners in the earliest stage of the AI transformation of the labor market. A recent analysis of U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data from economist Steve Rattner found that software developer was among the career categories that showed positive growth from May 2023 to May 2025, though it was merely in line with growth across all occupation and well below the pace of growth in traditionally blue-collar jobs associated with building AI data centers.

Anthropic researchers found that even with automation, humans are still needed to oversee that automation and require user input. But the researchers cautioned that it is "by no means certain that this pattern will persist into the future."

GitHub said in its report on pull requests that the as AI pushed more code into the world, and with it, more risks in the code, humans must be in a position to scale with the technology to police the AI's work. But that may not be possible forever. "As the amount of code grows, we must prevent more exposures and reduce the human effort required by those that remain, or else the volume of vulnerabilities introduced will become untenable," it wrote.

For the youngest workers, the software development field outlook remains uncertain. Stanford University's 2026 AI index found that employment in AI-exposed fields for those aged 22 to 25 has fallen 16% since the rise of generative AI, with those identified as early-career software developers seeing a larger decline in employment of 20% as older developer roles expand.

That shift has made the path into software development more difficult for recent graduates, even as demand rises for more experienced workers. Puri said students should build familiarity with AI tools but not neglect the skills that remain central when working with them. "Being able to use AI in your work and improve your efficiency is a great place to start," Puri said. "But communication, interpersonal skills and leadership are also really important," she added.

Puri said employers also have a role to play in preserving routes into the field. "Today's entry-level talent becomes tomorrow's senior experts," she said. "If employers don't build those pipelines now, they're not going to have senior talent they need 10 years down the line."

While forecasting job growth in the AI era is difficult, the long-term outlook for software developers remains positive, according to an August report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. It projects employment of software developers will grow 10% from 2025 to 2035, increasing from about 1.72 million to 1.89 million jobs and adding roughly 174,700 positions. (quoting @SteveRattner: "So far, A.I.'s losers are routine office jobs like data entry keyers and customer service reps.

Its winners are data scientists and the trades building the data centers like construction laborers and electricians.

virals.name: Andrej Karpathy
virals.text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. (quoting @karpathy: "Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.")

Much of it may never be fully read by a human," it stated.

Labor market researchers say that against this backdrop, the profession is evolving rather than disappearing. Data from Indeed Hiring Lab shows that U.S. software-development job postings have risen nearly 15% since February 2025, bucking both the overall job market and the coding data.

Some economic experts are pointing to the rebound in software job postings as confirmation for a glass half-full view of AI and the job market. "It wasn't that long ago that we were reading the headline that there will be no more need for software developers," Eric Kutcher, North America chair at McKinsey, said during a recent interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." Instead, he said, as companies are producing more code than ever before, software developers who work with AI remain in high demand. "We're seeing much more growth in the places we thought we were gonna see the biggest displacement," Kutcher said.

Recent research on AI and the future of jobs from McKinsey Global Institute notes that the earlier decline in the software developer field was not solely an AI story. While in recent years AI has been automating software-development tasks, the rebound comes after a steep drop from a 2022 hiring peak, when technology companies pulled back after a pandemic-era surge in hiring.

But even after the recovery, software-development job postings remain about 27.5% below their pre-pandemic level, according to Indeed Hiring Lab data. Importantly, the increase is concentrated in senior-level roles and more experienced AI-oriented positions. Indeed Hiring Lab found that senior roles accounted for 71% of the increase in software-development postings between May 2025 and May 2026. Job titles that mention AI accounted for 37% of the increase.

AI tools may be allowing companies to produce code more quickly than developers could on their own. GitHub leaders have said in the past that as much if not more than 80% of code could eventually be written by AI, especially as developers become more comfortable working with AI tools. But that also could mean the demand for workers is concentrated on those who can evaluate AI-generated code or problems and connect new tools to an organization's broader technology systems.

Sneha Puri, an economist at Indeed Hiring Lab, said companies are realizing that even if AI can handle some technical coding tasks, they still need developers to oversee that work, refine products and help clients integrate the technology into their day to day operations. One example, she said, is the growing need for workers who can help businesses apply AI tools beyond simply building them.

Early gains in AI era may not last, young workers remain at risk

Right now, factors like the ones cited by Puri are helping software developers to be among winners in the earliest stage of the AI transformation of the labor market. A recent analysis of U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data from economist Steve Rattner found that software developer was among the career categories that showed positive growth from May 2023 to May 2025, though it was merely in line with growth across all occupation and well below the pace of growth in traditionally blue-collar jobs associated with building AI data centers.

Anthropic researchers found that even with automation, humans are still needed to oversee that automation and require user input. But the researchers cautioned that it is "by no means certain that this pattern will persist into the future."

GitHub said in its report on pull requests that the as AI pushed more code into the world, and with it, more risks in the code, humans must be in a position to scale with the technology to police the AI's work. But that may not be possible forever. "As the amount of code grows, we must prevent more exposures and reduce the human effort required by those that remain, or else the volume of vulnerabilities introduced will become untenable," it wrote.

For the youngest workers, the software development field outlook remains uncertain. Stanford University's 2026 AI index found that employment in AI-exposed fields for those aged 22 to 25 has fallen 16% since the rise of generative AI, with those identified as early-career software developers seeing a larger decline in employment of 20% as older developer roles expand.

That shift has made the path into software development more difficult for recent graduates, even as demand rises for more experienced workers. Puri said students should build familiarity with AI tools but not neglect the skills that remain central when working with them. "Being able to use AI in your work and improve your efficiency is a great place to start," Puri said. "But communication, interpersonal skills and leadership are also really important," she added.

Puri said employers also have a role to play in preserving routes into the field. "Today's entry-level talent becomes tomorrow's senior experts," she said. "If employers don't build those pipelines now, they're not going to have senior talent they need 10 years down the line."

While forecasting job growth in the AI era is difficult, the long-term outlook for software developers remains positive, according to an August report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. It projects employment of software developers will grow 10% from 2025 to 2035, increasing from about 1.72 million to 1.89 million jobs and adding roughly 174,700 positions.
